title: Alberta Serious Incident Response Team clears Mounties in death after Taser deployed
article: The provincial police watchdog has cleared Mounties in the case of a man who died last year after a Leduc crime spree ended when he was zapped with a Taser.

The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) was assigned to investigate the Aug. 2, 2013, arrest of 27-year old Marc Andre Fontaine in Leduc. His death was attributed by the medical examiner to exited delirium as a result of cocaine toxicity.

Excited delirium is a condition in which an individual exhibits bizarre and often violent and aggressive behaviour, "superhuman" strength and stamina, a lack of response to verbal commands and pain and constant motion and hyperactivity. It generally occurs as a consequence of illicit drug abuse, particularly cocaine, although other drugs can trigger the syndrome as well.

ASIRT investigators said Fontaine -- a father of three -- was seen in public that afternoon exhibiting bizarre behaviour and appeared to be extremely pale with purple lips. About 9:30 p.m., at his home, Fontaine was also observed as foaming at the mouth, gritting his teeth and growling. Witnesses described Fontaine as assaulting his roommate and then fleeing the residence.

Between that time and when police came into contact with Fontaine at 10 p.m., he was involved in breaking through a door into a neighbouring residence while the owner slept, the theft of an unattended vehicle and disturbances at two convenience stores.

ASIRT says Fontaine's behaviour at one convenience store was described as a "rampage" which included the assault of an employee. Fontaine fled the second convenience store in the stolen vehicle and was described by witnesses to be driving at excessive speeds, proceeding through red lights and driving on the wrong side of the road. He arrived at a Leduc Petro Canada service station crashing through a steel barricade.

Fontaine then entered a stranger's vehicle that was parked adjacent to the gas pumps causing the owner to flee the vehicle. He moved to the driver's seat where police found him when they arrived at the gas station.

One officer opened the driver's door and attempted to speak to Fontaine. Fontaine subsequently punched the officer and a violent struggle occurred. Two additional officers arrived and attempted to assist in removing him from the vehicle but were unsuccessful.

A police officer readied his Conducted Energy Device (CED) and warned Fontaine that the Taser was going to be deployed. He continued to grip the steering wheel at which time the CED was deployed in stun mode to the right side of his torso. Fontaine momentarily released his grip and the CED was turned off.

ASIRT investigators say Fontaine regained his grip on the steering wheel. Having turned the CED off, the officer turned it back on and applied it a second time, in stun mode, to Fontaine's right side at which point he released the steering wheel and was pulled from the vehicle.

The violent struggle continued outside the vehicle. Notwithstanding the three officers and two civilian witnesses who attempted to assist, Fontaine was uncontrollable, displayed exceptional strength and could not be placed in handcuffs. An officer employed a carotid control hold at which point control was gained and Fontaine was finally handcuffed. Within seconds of releasing the hold, Fontaine coughed and was noted to be breathing. He was raised to a seated position and appeared to be conscious.
But between one to two minutes later, ASIRT investigators say, Fontaine went into medical distress, appeared to stop breathing and ultimately went into cardiac arrest.

Notwithstanding efforts by members, emergency medical personnel and medical staff, he did not recover and was placed on life support and at 5:28 a.m. on Aug. 4, 2013, he was pronounced dead at the Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton.

Susan D. Hughson, acting ASIRT executive director, reviewed the completed independent investigation conducted by ASIRT and has concluded that at the time police dealt with Fontaine, they were lawfully placed and acting reasonably in the execution of their duties.
